t: A Fun Learning Game For Every Age And Subject
q: It’s a review game you can play for virtually any subject and any grade level. And your students will have a blast.
Step #1 – Write each letter of the alphabet on large index cards, one letter per card. Create two sets, one written in red marker and one in blue.
Step #6 – Call two groups up to compete. To begin, each group must stand side-by-side, silent, and facing the room with their hands clasped in front of them.
Step #9 – The first team to have every member holding a card silently while spelling out the word correctly and facing the class gets 15 points.
Step #10 – If the other team is also able to spell the word out correctly, they receive 10 points. This encourages both teams to finish.
Just do so in your host voice and never break character. It’s a time for learning, yes. But it’s also for having fun.

t: The Pain of Exclusion Is Real
q: Whenever people feel abandoned, rejected, or disconfirmed, they experience an intense pain not unlike the physical pain we endure after being injured.
In fact, social and physical pain register in the same area of the brain and share many of the same symptoms.
Unlike the physical pain of an ailment or sprain, social pain can linger long past an incident, sometimes for days, months, and even years.
The truth is, even these wayward and highly resistant colleagues don't want to be excluded, ignored, or rejected by the team and the team leader.
Used as a last resort, leaders who purposely exclude team members will often find a huge shift in their willingness to play along.
The social pain dissipates quickly once it is done teaching resistant colleagues what really matters. Pain is one way we learn.

t: Two Principles for Normalizing Struggle in a Given Classroom
q: In one of the sessions, we were looking at the mechanics of creating secondary classrooms in which struggle is normal and — dare we hope for it? — even desirable for all students.

If struggle is something that many kids in a class do not normally experience, then, definitionally, struggle is not normal in that classroom. As a result, in such places the students who do struggle will tend toward demotivation due to an awareness that they don't Belong.
And so the "struggle is normal" classroom has to be one in which the bar is set very high. This doesn't mean that you only need high expectations to help students grow.

Struggle alone, however, does not motivation make. No human being can struggle in futility indefinitely. If a person is to persist in effort over the long term, that person must gain a sense, amidst the strain, that the effort is paying off in some way.

Teach, model, and reinforce the sub-skills and prior knowledge bits that make growth toward your high expectations possible. As the teacher, define success relentlessly as growth toward the high bar you've set.

t: When Aspirations Don't Line Up With Skill
q: Colleagues with low self-awareness are also commonly blind to how others see and judge them and their skills.
Convincing a colleague with low self-awareness that they do not have the skills or talents to achieve their aspirations is nearly impossible.
Good leaders don't make a frontal assault on this gap when they are dealing with an unaware team member.
Leaders collect the perceptions of others and then allow the unaware team member to stare reality in the eye and accept or reject it.
Even for those without self-awareness, just seeing how a large swath of colleagues perceives them becomes irrefutable.
Changing the awareness of those without it is a herculean task. The first step toward this change is understanding.

t: How To Handle Being Hated For Great Classroom Management
q: If you’re exceptional at classroom management, your colleagues will hate you for it.
The truth is, it doesn’t matter the endeavor. If you pursue excellence in any area of your life , many people, including your closest friends, won’t like it.
These are the sorriest souls who, as Thoreau mused, “are living lives of quiet desperation,” only feeling satisfaction in seeing you stumble.

Let them fade into your background. Highlight the beauty and inspiration around you and allow them to fall away from your attention. Do not attempt to get your own revenge. It will drag you down to their level, which is what they want.

You’re merely forcing them to confront the truth. It tells them oh so subtly that you’re on to them. You don’t have to say anything, though hello is okay. Be pleasant, but hold their eyes until they look away.
Funny, when you get to a certain level of success—undeniable success—again in any endeavor, everyone wants to be your friend. Those same vampires become sycophants, hoping to steal some of your mojo.
Of the many dysfunctions suffered by organizations, perhaps none is more common or corrosive than silos.
In a highly siloed organization, leaders don't talk to one another. They simply don't believe they have any reason to.

Breaking down silos depends on defining shared accountability. When leaders are jointly responsible for outcomes and own results together, they quickly learn to drop the pretenses and begin to collaborate.
In order for this strategy to have a lasting impact, the projects must be significant and the leaders involved should be highly credible within their segment of the organization.
When siloed leaders suggest that creating joint accountability makes no sense, don't believe them. They simply need a push and a spark of creative insight to see things anew.

t: Common Misperceptions Regarding Moments of Genuine Connection
q: Once folks start trying to implement tracking attempted moments of genuine connection (MGCs), there are a few misperceptions that start to crop up.
If MGC attempts become some "got-to-do-it" thing that external forces are pushing onto our plates, it's pretty likely that we'll end up missing the G in MGC. They won't be genuine.

To fix this, you've got to find rhythms and routines that make MGCs make sense to you. Maybe all of your MGC attempts are during class passing times; maybe they are all during an independent work portion of your lesson.

For MGC attempts to have their best effects on the Credibility belief, they need to be roughly balanced into both personal and academic categories. We want to send signals that indicate our Care, holistically, for each of our students.

While lots of MGC attempts are going to give you the warm fuzzies and feel pretty effortless, it's unreasonable to expect that you'll have an easy time connecting with all of your students. Sometimes these are awkward.
Charming, stylish, and often athletically talented, entitled students believe they’re special and not subject to the same boundaries and expectations as others.
It’s terrible for them. One day the piper will come calling requiring skill, discipline, and hard work and they’ll have none of these. In the end, they pay. And they pay dearly.
Promise to follow through for all students from day one, damn the torpedoes, and everything becomes much easier.
They’ll act angry for awhile and when that doesn’t work they’ll lay on the charm. You must resist. Smiling is fine, but don’t say much when they begin to justify, cajole, and plead.
Treating some students differently because of their personality or athletic ability or any other reason is discriminatory. Plain and simple.
So many of these students find out too late that their entitlement doesn’t last beyond eighth grade or high school, and they can’t handle it. They’re unprepared for it.
Rather than assuming everyone feels the same as him and is able to identify feelings he's able to identify, Rogers explicitly says, again and again: "Do you feel that feeling? That's a good one.
The bulk of our classrooms suffer for lack of explicit instruction. We are tragically presumptuous about what our students understand.
And second, Rogers is So. Doggone. Confident. He knows that what he's offering his students — the kids viewing his show — is a timeless good.

We work in a medium — school — that's one of the few remaining commonplaces in the communities wherein we live. Television's commonplaceness is gone now, replaced by an algorithmically individualized, numberless, creators-driven Internet.

No — just like Rogers was responsible for reminding himself of the good feelings possible in television, so too are we responsible, in a world gone mad, for reminding ourselves of the Why behind what we do.
Most frequent gamblers are indifferent to loss. While they prefer to win, that's not the real goal behind placing bets.
The so-called "action" of gambling consumes 100 percent of a gambler's attention and creates an intensity of experience that gamblers crave.
Failure doesn't bother them nearly as much as it does others because it is equally as captivating as success.
Good leaders identify the excitement-seeking intrapreneurs who will take unnecessary chances with house money.
Checking in frequently with the risk-takers and giving them clear parameters as to what they can and cannot do serve to help everyone.
A check on reality is all a risk-taker really needs. Leaders guard the gate, while letting everyone through.

t: We're the Fork to the Community's Farm
q: One of the strategies I emphasize in my workshops is a bit odd-sounding: "An Apologist Winsome and Sure." The gist is this: we want to become the kinds of teachers who relentlessly, repetitively, confidently, and creatively explain to students why what they're doing in our classes matters.
An apologist teacher expects that students will ask things like, "Why is this worth my time?" They're not offended by skepticism.

And so the FFA/food and nutrition teacher I'm talking about, at the end of the workshop, handed me a piece of paper with her takeaways from the workshop, and under the Apologetics column she wrote these things: Food sanitation saves or costs lives.
Communicating deep Value — it's a thing we envisioned ourselves doing when we decided to become teachers. So often, I find that my work comes down to this: remember that impulse? Go back!
So what are your one-liners, colleague? Your versions of, "We are the fork to the community's farm?
In the history of organizational success, the enterprises that dominate tend to flawlessly execute on ideas that were created elsewhere.

The xenophobia of ideas "not invented here" cripples organizations over the long run, and often allows competitors to destroy longstanding value by embracing better ideas and executing them with polish.
The reality is that the leader's unwillingness to acknowledge or value the work of others outside the team is a form of arrogance that weakens the very thing it is meant to protect.
Everyone wants one. Everyone needs one. But no one wants to use someone else's.
Thankfully, most team success solutions and practices are more like toothpaste than toothbrushes.
It's time for the monopoly of "not invented here" to end in your organization. Not everything is a toothbrush.

t: Why Low Standards Are Destroying Our Schools
q: Lowering standards removes purpose. It weakens pride in excellence. It encourages students not to care and feeds the growing malaise and troubling misbehavior infecting our schools.

The best thing for mental health is having purpose . It’s having goals and aspirations bigger than themselves and high standards to strive for. When you take this away from students and ease their way you leave them rudderless.

The result is that students will look for purpose elsewhere – whether online, in gangs or drugs, or in extreme misbehavior born of frustration and emptiness. Those that don’t find it struggle with depression, anxiety, and a gnawing sense of nihilism.

But all the while they’re crushing our students. They’re snuffing out their motivation and any joy of learning. They appease and excuse those who disrupt and bully, and leave scores of students afraid, silent, and demoralized.
It should be focused on how to elevate standards, improve teacher content knowledge, teach compelling lessons, and effectively manage a classroom.

t: How to Feel Less Nuts This School Year
q: Instead, we've got to apprentice ourselves to two broad areas of practice: Depressurization of self. Simplification of workload.
Depressurization of self requires a clear eye on what a self actually is. I'm pretty convinced that we're five-part creatures: physical, intellectual, emotional, relational, and volitional.
When you're stressed at work and in life, it's easy to justify staying up late so that you can blow off steam; this feels good for a bit, but it makes waking up the next day more of a drag.
If you're smart and aware of your surroundings, there will always be too much to do. And so you must become more than smart; you must become wise.
Both are part of the journey this year, friend. And all the years after. We won't regret time contemplating, practicing, and playing in these two sandboxes.

t: Receptivity to New Ideas Is the Real Problem
q: The problem is not the ability for organizations to elicit new and advantageous ideas. The issue is one of receptivity.
Too much innovation can threaten the comfortable seat of those with status and power.
Team members learn quickly to keep their best ideas to themselves, while leaders continue the charade of promoting innovative thinking without much success.
The most innovative ideas are commonly hidden in plain sight. They sit right under our noses.
No promises or commitments have to be given. This takes the pressure off leaders who feel threatened by the need to act on ideas they honestly think are inferior.
You see, whatever misbehavior you justify, you accept. If you view talking instead of listening or focusing on work as just who your students are, then it will never stop.
Here at SCM, we believe that the entire premise that students are just the way they are, no matter the behavior, is hogwash. You decide how our students behave, not the other way around.
But like every area of classroom management, eliminating unwanted talking is simply a function of knowledge. It’s a matter of knowing what to do and then doing it.
When you know your approach is right and best for them, and you know you won’t accept anything less, then your students will know it too. They’ll hear it in your voice and see it on your face.

Talking when your students are supposed to be listening or working independently is not “just who they are.” It’s not a learning style or a personality trait. It’s not a cutesy social quirk or an acceptable excuse.

t: Are Your Greatest Weaknesses Also Your Greatest Strengths?
q: An aversion to risks can provide much needed caution in a life-threatening event.
When we let our strengths grab ahold of us without being checked, they become a weakness.
Most weaknesses become dysfunctional precisely because we avoid the situations that allow us to conquer them.
The weakness of taking feedback poorly becomes amplified the more we shun criticism.
The best leaders work on their weaknesses by applying them. Let's face it. Most weaknesses never disappear entirely.
We don't overcome weakness nearly as much as we commit to making them more productive.
